Rose-ringed parakeet (Psittacula krameri) is a medium-sized parrot species that has successfully colonized urban environments across much of its expansive introduced range. Freshly laid eggs are incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a temperature that is critical for normal embryonic development, and hatch after a period of approximately 23 days [ab = approximately 23 days]. This incubation duration is broadly consistent with that reported for other Psittacula species of comparable body size, though it can vary slightly depending on local ambient conditions and the attentiveness of the incubating female. The altricial nestlings that emerge from these incubated eggs weigh just 7 grams [Wwb = 7 grams] at hatching, a remarkably low neonatal mass that reflects the substantial energetic investment still required from the parents during the subsequent brooding and provisioning phases. These tiny chicks, initially covered in sparse down, depend entirely on their parents for thermoregulation and a steady supply of regurgitated crop milk and partially digested seeds to fuel their rapid growth trajectory.

As the nestling period progresses, the altricial chicks undergo a pronounced phase of rapid mass gain, transitioning from their initial hatchling weight to a substantially larger size before they are ready to leave the nest. Under the thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic period in this species (41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]), fledging, defined as the point at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and departs the nest, occurs at 45.5 days after hatching [tx = 45.5 days after hatching]. This developmental milestone is followed by a period of post-fledging dependence during which the parents continue to provision the fledgling while it refines its flight skills and learns to locate food sources independently. The absolute mass and growth rate during this stage are tightly linked to the quality and quantity of food provided by the parents, with experimentally supplemented broods sometimes reaching the asymptotic mass more quickly. The transition to nutritional independence is therefore a critical phase that heavily influences first-year survival probabilities in this species across its varied introduced habitats.

Following the successful fledging of their young, breeding adult Rose-ringed parakeets exhibit a well-defined reproductive schedule that is closely tied to local resource availability. The age at which a young bird first reaches gonadal maturation and becomes a reproductively active adult occurs at 136.5 days after hatching [tp = 136.5 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the typical body temperature associated with active metabolism in this species. This relatively rapid attainment of sexual maturity is characteristic of many successful avian invaders, allowing populations to expand quickly following initial establishment. However, in wild populations, the actual age at which individuals initiate their first reproductive effort is often delayed beyond the physiological minimum due to social constraints, including competition for limited nest cavities and the need to establish a pair bond. The onset of reproductive activation is therefore a plastic trait in this species, modulated by the density of conspecifics and the availability of suitable nesting resources in both native and introduced ranges.

The first successful breeding attempt, which represents the time since birth at first brood, typically occurs at 730 days after hatching [tR = 730 days after hatching] for individuals experiencing the thermal regime of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This delay between the attainment of puberty at just over four months and the actual commencement of reproduction reflects the challenges associated with securing a suitable nest cavity and a compatible mate in a competitive environment. Nesting adults exhibit strong site fidelity, often returning to the same cavity year after year, which confers advantages through familiarity with local food resources and predator refuges. Once a breeding pair is established, females lay a standard clutch of eggs and undertake the majority of incubation duties, while males are primarily responsible for provisioning the brooding female and later the developing chicks. The overall annual reproductive output is constrained not only by physiological limits but also by the duration of the breeding season, which itself is influenced by temperature and rainfall patterns.

Reproductive output in Rose-ringed parakeet is best described by the combination of clutch size and the frequency of nesting attempts. Females typically lay a clutch of 4 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 4 eggs per nesting attempt], and under favorable conditions, a pair may successfully raise 1 brood per year [F_R_i = 1 brood per year]. The ultimate adult body mass attained by these birds is 140 grams [Wwi = 140 grams], placing them at the upper end of the size range for the genus Psittacula. Remarkably, the maximum recorded longevity in the species is 34 years [am = 34 years] when maintained at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], a lifespan that far exceeds that of many similarly sized passerines and reflects a slow life-history pace relative to body size. This combination of a moderately high reproductive rate and an exceptionally long adult lifespan provides a powerful demographic engine that helps explain the species' remarkable success as a colonist on multiple continents.
